lesson.title: Turning Sunlight into Sugar: The Big Picture of Photosynthesis
lesson.summary: Photosynthesis uses light energy to drive the thermodynamically uphill conversion of carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen, in two linked stages housed in different compartments of the chloroplast.
lesson.body:
Nearly every calorie of usable energy in the biosphere can be traced back to a single kind of chemical transformation: the conversion of light energy into the energy stored in chemical bonds. Photosynthesis is the process that performs this conversion, and in its most general form it can be summarized by one overall equation: six molecules of carbon dioxide plus six molecules of water, with light energy as input, yield one molecule of glucose plus six molecules of oxygen gas. Behind that simple equation lies an elegant two stage system housed inside the chloroplast.

This transformation makes sense only in light of basic thermodynamics. Glucose is a high energy, relatively ordered molecule compared to carbon dioxide and water, so building it does not happen spontaneously; it requires a substantial energy input, which is exactly the role light plays. Photosynthesis takes low entropy, high energy photons streaming in from the sun and uses that energy to drive an energetically uphill, endergonic reaction, converting it into the more stable, storable chemical energy of covalent bonds. Cellular respiration later reverses this, releasing that stored energy in usable form, but photosynthesis is what puts the energy there in the first place.

The process happens in two linked stages inside the chloroplast, each occurring in a different compartment. The light dependent reactions take place in and across the thylakoid membranes, stacked internal membranes organized into grana, where pigments capture light energy and use it to produce ATP and NADPH while splitting water and releasing oxygen as a byproduct. The Calvin cycle, sometimes called the light independent reactions, takes place in the stroma, the fluid surrounding the thylakoids, where the ATP and NADPH generated by the light reactions power the fixation of carbon dioxide into sugar.

This division of labor mirrors the chloroplast's own internal architecture: the thylakoid membrane provides a closed compartment across which the light reactions can build a proton gradient, while the surrounding stroma provides the aqueous space and enzymes needed for carbon fixation chemistry. Nothing about this two stage arrangement is arbitrary. It reflects the fact that capturing light energy and using that energy to build sugar are chemically very different jobs, one built around membrane bound electron transport, the other around soluble enzyme catalyzed carbon chemistry, and the chloroplast's structure keeps each job in its own compartment.

Photosynthesis is ultimately what allows plants, algae, and cyanobacteria to serve as the primary producers at the base of nearly every food web, converting solar energy that no animal can use directly into chemical energy that can be eaten, digested, and metabolized. It is also the source of essentially all atmospheric oxygen. The chapters that follow zoom into each stage in turn, beginning with the pigments that make capturing light possible in the first place.
